claim.text: For networks within the same design family (architectures that share stage structure and repeating blocks), a winning ticket (a subnetwork characterized by a binary mask and weights rewound to an early training point) found by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on one network (the source) can be transformed into a competitive winning ticket for another network in the same family (the target) of different depth by mindfully replicating (for deeper targets), dropping (for shallower targets), and re-ordering the source network's layers/blocks and their corresponding binary mask, producing a subnetwork for the target that attains performance nearly as high as a winning ticket obtained by running IMP directly on the target.

Applying Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) to transform Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found winning tickets across ResNet and VGG depths on CIFAR-10 yields transferred tickets whose trained accuracies are nearly the same as those of IMP-found winning tickets on the target models across a wide range of sparsities (fraction of zero weights).
for ResNet-32 at 90% sparsity, the dense model accuracy is 93.83%; E-LTH transferred tickets incur an accuracy drop of -0.96% relative to the dense model
For ResNet-56 at 90% sparsity, dense accuracy is 94.51% and E-LTH drop is -0.50%
Across multiple ResNet depths and VGG-13/16/19 transforms, ETTs consistently outperform alternative pruning-at-initialization methods, particularly at high sparsities.

On ImageNet at sparsity (fraction of zero weights) 73.79%, Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets for ResNet architectures attain top-1 accuracies close to Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found tickets and substantially above pruning-at-initialization baselines.

dense model top-1 accuracies: ResNet-18 69.96%, ResNet-26 72.56%, ResNet-34 73.77%; IMP accuracies: 70.22%, 72.94%, 74.20% respectively; ETTs transferred from ResNet-26 yield ResNet-18: 68.17%, ResNet-34: 73.37%; ETTs transferred from ResNet-18 yield ResNet-26: 71.29%, ResNet-34: 71.86%.

Compared to SNIP (62.23%, 67.51%, 69.35%) and GraSP (62.85%, 67.24%, 69.23%), Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets are much closer to Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found tickets.

Across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet experiments, transferred tickets produced by Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) substantially outperform state-of-the-art pruning-at-initialization methods and one-shot magnitude pruning baselines at matched sparsity levels (fraction of zero weights).

for ResNet-26 at 73.79% sparsity, SNIP = 67.51%, GraSP = 67.24%, one-shot magnitude pruning = 68.51%, while ETTs transferred from ResNet-18 achieve 71.29% and Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) = 72.94%.
On CIFAR-10, similar superior performance gaps are observed across multiple ResNet and VGG depth transforms at sparsities above 80%.

Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH)—where Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) is run once on a source model and Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) produce tickets for multiple targets—achieves comparable accuracies to dynamic sparse training (DST) methods while being cost-competitive or cheaper when amortized across multiple target architectures.

Representative comparisons on ImageNet with ResNet-18/26/34 at 73.79% sparsity show E-LTH accuracies: ResNet-18 68.17%, ResNet-26 72.94%, ResNet-34 73.37%, versus RigL with 5x training (RigL-5x) accuracies: 69.59%, 72.66%, 73.88%.
RigL (a DST method) requires up to 1.30x normalized FLOPs for ResNet-34, with FLOPs normalized by the FLOPs of one-pass standard dense training on ResNet-34.

E-LTH, using ResNet-26 as source, uses 2.77x FLOPs (normalized by the FLOPs of one-pass standard dense training on ResNet-34) once for source IMP plus small per-target training (0.14x for ResNet-18, 0.20x for ResNet-26, 0.26x for ResNet-34).
Against DPF (dynamic model pruning with feedback) on CIFAR-10, E-LTH matches or slightly improves accuracy drops at 90% and 95% sparsity.
E-LTH uses lower total FLOPs (1.26 billion FLOPs vs 1.49 billion FLOPs) to obtain sparse models across five ResNet variants (ResNet-14, -20, -32, -44, -56).
When transferring winning tickets across ResNet depths, one should choose minimal replication units consistent with model structure.
When transferring winning tickets across ResNet depths, one should preserve number of stages (groups of blocks delimited by down-sampling), down-sampling blocks, and input/output layers.

When stretching (deepening), one should prefer replicating more distinct source blocks fewer times (replicate unique units) rather than repeating the same unit many times, to better preserve per-stage sparsity (fraction of zero weights per stage).
Replication ordering can be interpolation (replicated block inserted immediately after its source block) or appending (replicated blocks appended after the last block) with comparable performance.
When transferring winning tickets across ResNet depths, one should prefer replicating or dropping later blocks less aggressively and avoid dropping too many early blocks.
Dropping many early blocks degrades accuracy.

The design rules for Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) regarding minimal replication units, preserving stages/down-sampling blocks/input-output layers, replication strategy when stretching, replication ordering, and how aggressively to replicate or drop blocks matter more at high sparsity levels.
Elastic Ticket Transformations can transfer winning tickets that include fully-connected layers and can be combined with dataset transfer.

For VGG variants with differing numbers of fully-connected (FC) layers and for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) of varying widths on MNIST, the Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis approach (E-LTH) transfers at 89.26% sparsity (fraction of zero weights) with ≤0.21% accuracy differences relative to directly trained winning tickets.
Transferring tickets across datasets and architectures shows that dataset shifts cause an accuracy drop and architectural shifts cause another drop, but these drops do not simply add linearly.

For example, transferring a ResNet-20 winning ticket from SVHN to CIFAR-10 and from ResNet-20 to ResNet-32 simultaneously yields a 3.55% net accuracy drop compared to the Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning baseline on the target.
For ImageNet to CIFAR-10 transfer, Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) from ResNet-18 to ResNet-18 achieve 95.40% top-1 accuracy.
For ImageNet to CIFAR-10 transfer, Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) from ResNet-18 to ResNet-26 achieve 95.16% top-1 accuracy, showing small drops.

Transferred tickets via Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) can exhibit linear mode connectivity (the property that a linear interpolation of the parameters of two independently trained models achieves test accuracy comparable to the endpoints) similar to Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found winning tickets when the source and target are close in depth.
The stability of linear mode connectivity of transferred tickets via Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) degrades as the depth difference between the source and target increases.
ETTs transferred from ResNet-20 to ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity show a maximum interpolation accuracy drop of 8.72%
ETTs (Elastic Ticket Transformations) transferred from ResNet-14 to ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity show a much larger maximal drop of 69.72% in interpolation accuracy.
IMP (Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning)-found tickets remain stable under linear interpolation, with a maximal drop near zero.
ETTs (Elastic Ticket Transformations) better preserve linear connectivity when source and target belong to the same loss basin (smaller depth gap).
Across multiple ResNet depths and VGG-13/16/19 transforms, ETTs consistently outperform the alternative pruning-at-initialization methods SNIP and GraSP, particularly at high sparsities.

On ImageNet at sparsity (fraction of zero weights) 73.79%, Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets for ResNet architectures attain top-1 accuracies close to Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found tickets and substantially above the pruning-at-initialization baselines SNIP and GraSP.

Across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet experiments, transferred tickets produced by Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) substantially outperform the state-of-the-art pruning-at-initialization methods SNIP and GraSP and one-shot magnitude pruning baselines at matched sparsity levels (fraction of zero weights).

When transferring winning tickets across ResNet depths, one should choose residual blocks as the minimal replication unit for ResNets, and a convolutional layer plus normalization layer as the minimal replication unit for VGG, consistent with model structure.

For the VGG variants VGG-13-2, VGG-13-3, and VGG-13-5, differing in numbers of fully-connected (FC) layers, and for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) of varying widths on MNIST, the Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis approach (E-LTH) transfers at 89.26% sparsity (fraction of zero weights) with ≤0.21% accuracy differences relative to directly trained winning tickets.
